status_summary: No single plan of the kind described has been issued; the executive branch has taken separate steps that point in different directions. On 2025-05-13 Commerce announced it would not enforce and would rescind the January 2025 AI diffusion rule and issued guidance that included cloud providers training AI models for China-linked entities as a red flag; GAO found on 2026-05-12 that the non-enforcement policy is a rule under the Congressional Review Act and that no rescission rule had been published. Executive Order 14320 (signed 2025-07-23) promotes exports of full-stack U.S. AI packages and does not name China. A BIS rule of 2026-01-15 moved licenses for certain advanced chips to China and Macau from presumed denial to case-by-case review, while conditioning them on know-your-customer screening against unauthorized remote access, disclosure of remote and cloud (IaaS) end users in countries of concern, and limits on cloud providers' customers. The House passed the Remote Access Security Act (H.R. 2683) 369 to 22 on 2026-01-12; it and its Senate companion S. 3519 sit in Senate Banking with no action. No general rule on remote or cloud access to controlled chips was found in the Federal Register.

timeline.event: Commerce/BIS announced the start of rescission of the January 2025 AI diffusion rule, told enforcement officials not to enforce it, and issued guidance on Chinese advanced chips and on chip supply to cloud providers training AI models for China-linked entities.

Executive Order 14320, Promoting the Export of the American AI Technology Stack (signed 2025-07-23), was published; it sets up an AI exports program for full-stack packages including cloud services and does not name China.
The House passed the Remote Access Security Act (H.R. 2683), 369 to 22 (roll call 13); it was referred to Senate Banking on 2026-01-13.

BIS published a final rule (91 FR 1684, effective the same day) moving license review for certain advanced chips to China and Macau from presumption of denial to case-by-case, conditioned on know-your-customer procedures to prevent unauthorized remote access, a list of intended remote and IaaS end users in countries of concern, and checks on IaaS providers' customers.
GAO decided (B-337935) that Commerce's May 2025 announcement is a rule under the Congressional Review Act and noted no formal rescission rule or replacement had been published.

title: Plan to stop U.S. entities contributing to China's AI goals, including via cloud computing
uncertainties: The BIS May 2025 announcement and guidance were read through the GAO decision and a law-firm alert; the BIS pages were not opened. The Action Plan (July 2025) has no provision on adversary access to cloud compute; its location-verification and end-use monitoring items are chip-diversion measures and are not counted as events. Reports that Commerce is drafting a rule on remote access, and that the prior administration's foundry due diligence and cloud know-your-customer requirements are not being enforced, come from one trade news article and are not events. The 2026-01-15 rule's know-your-customer and remote-access conditions apply only to license applications under that rule, not to cloud providers generally. The BIS rule of 2026-07-14 giving the UAE more favorable export treatment (license-free access to advanced computing items for approved UAE entities) concerns a partner country, not China, and was moved out of the timeline as context only. Federal Register queries for cloud and remote access among BIS documents returned only Entity List rules and the two rules named; the Entity List rules were not read for AI-specific listings. The stage is a judgment: the only tightening measures are a House-passed bill and license conditions inside a rule that loosens China chip licensing, and no plan exists, so proposed 15 with a partial match is used; in_progress 25 is the alternative if the license conditions are read as an operative step. The Mandate does not specify a mechanism.
